summary: Explores how Segment Routing over IPv6 Segment Identifiers relate to the IPv6 Addressing Architecture, since SIDs look and often act like IPv6 addresses. It also allocates a dedicated prefix for SRv6 SIDs. It is informational.

eli5.summary: SRv6 stops look like street addresses but work a little differently. This explains how, and sets aside a block of addresses just for them.

subtitle: A dedicated IPv6 prefix block for SRv6 Segment Identifiers

tldr.problem: SRv6 Segment Identifiers (SIDs) look like IPv6 addresses and appear in IPv6 Destination Address fields, but they follow a different structure and are not assigned to interfaces in the way RFC 4291 specifies.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC clarifies that SIDs are routing prefixes, not interface addresses, and allocates the /16 prefix block 5f00::/16 as a dedicated space where SRv6 SIDs can be identified and distinguished from regular IPv6 addresses.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can now use this prefix to filter and protect SRv6 domains at their edges, improving security and simplifying failure modes.

today: RFC 9602 is Informational and remains current as the authoritative source for the SRv6 SID address block allocation. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.content:
Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6, defined in RFC 8754) is a source-routing technique that uses IPv6 as the data plane. In SRv6, a router specifies a path by putting Segment Identifiers (SIDs) into the IPv6 Destination Address field. Each SID represents a routing instruction—typically, "go to this switch and do this function."

Because SIDs appear in IPv6 Destination Addresses, they resemble IPv6 addresses. However, they are not assigned to interfaces and do not follow all the rules in RFC 4291 (the IPv6 Addressing Architecture). Instead, they are pure forwarding constructs used within an SR Domain. This document clarifies their role and allocates a special IPv6 prefix block to make them identifiable.
sections.eli5: SRv6 uses addresses to give directions, but these are not real addresses like your computer's IP; they are routing instructions. The RFC explains the difference and sets aside some special numbers for them.

sections.title: SRv6 SID Structure and IPv6 Forwarding
sections.content:
An SRv6 SID is a 128-bit value structured as LOC:FUNCT:ARG, where the Locator (LOC) occupies the L most significant bits, the Function code (FUNCT) follows for F bits, and Arguments (ARG) fill A bits. The remaining 128 − L − F − A bits are zeros. The Locator is assigned to a node within an SR Domain; it acts like a routing prefix.

When a transit node (one not running SRv6) receives a packet destined to an SID, it simply performs longest-prefix matching on the Locator and forwards the packet accordingly. The node does not treat the SID as an interface address. This decouples SRv6 routing from the IPv6 Addressing Architecture requirements, making SIDs compatible with variable-length prefix forwarding as described in RFC 7608 (BCP 198).
sections.eli5: An SID is like an address split into parts: a location code, a function code, and arguments. Routers just look at the location part and forward onward—they do not care about the rest.

sections.title: Compressed SIDs and Address Format Flexibility
sections.content:
Compressed SIDs (C-SIDs) pack multiple SIDs into a single 128-bit address slot. A node processes C-SIDs by extracting the ARG portion of the current Destination Address and using it to derive the next address. Crucially, the Locator Block at the start of the address is not modified by this process.

Because SRv6 operation is restricted to SR-aware nodes within an SR Domain, and the Locator Block is preserved, changes to the Destination Address do not violate IPv6 data plane expectations on non-SR-aware transit nodes. Those nodes simply continue to forward by longest-prefix matching on the Locator.
sections.eli5: Clever SRv6 nodes can squeeze multiple routing steps into one address by reusing part of it. The key location code stays the same so regular routers still know where to send it.

sections.title: Dedicated Prefix Allocation and Security Benefits
sections.content:
IANA has allocated the prefix block 5f00::/16 for SRv6 SIDs. This block explicitly signals that addresses within it may not comply with RFC 4291 addressing semantics. It provides security through isolation: operators at the edge of an SR Domain can filter packets destined to this block, ensuring that SRv6 packets do not leak to non-SR-aware domains and that hostile SRv6 traffic cannot enter.

As of publication, global DNS SHOULD NOT reference addresses in this block. Future specifications are expected to define conventions for using this space. Deployments that do not use this dedicated prefix must take extra care at domain boundaries to prevent SRv6 packet leakage and intrusion.
sections.eli5: The network community set aside a special block of numbers just for SRv6: 5f00::/16. This makes it easy to spot SRv6 traffic at network edges and block it if needed for safety.

left.desc: Assigned to an interface. Used by the host to indicate its identity and location.

right.title: SRv6 SID
right.desc: A forwarding instruction. Contains locator (where), function (what), and arguments (details). Only meaningful within the SR Domain.
